posts.author: Dr. Mohamed Abdellaziz Hmad
posts.title: Pilot
posts.body:
I was young enough that the souq felt enormous, and old enough to sense that my father had brought me there for a reason, though he never said what it was.

We left early, while Ksar Hellal was still waking up. Other towns wake to birds or church bells. Ours woke to machines. Somewhere behind the walls the looms were already going, that steady metallic clatter you stop hearing after a few days and start missing the moment you leave. The streets smelled of strong coffee and warm bread, and under that, the dry, dusty, slightly sweet smell of cotton. Grow up in a textile town and that smell is home.

My father walked with his hands behind his back, in no hurry, nodding at people on both sides. A walk to the market was never just a walk. Every few steps someone called his name, and each call meant a handshake, a question about the family, a remark about the weather, a joke. I only understood much later that this was already business. Nobody was selling anything yet, but everyone was being looked at, remembered, and sized up.

Then the old souq opened in front of us, like a different country.

The sound hit first. Dozens of voices over each other in Tunisian dialect, shouting prices, laughing, arguing the half-serious way people argue when they already know how it ends. Carts rattled over the uneven stones. A metal shutter screeched up somewhere. Someone dropped a crate, someone else cursed it, a third person laughed.

Then the colors. Thread everywhere, in cones and spools and tangled hanks, stacked in open crates along the walls. Indigo next to bright red, mustard next to bleached white, and a dull grey that I learned later was just undyed cotton thread, still waiting to become something. Bales of raw cotton sat near the entrances in rough sacking, a few already torn open so buyers could see inside. White tufts drifted through the air like slow little snowflakes and landed on shoulders, on hair, on the dark wool of the men’s jackets. By noon everyone wore a light dusting of cotton and nobody noticed.

What I remember best is the men’s hands. Thick, cracked, stained at the fingertips from dye and oil, never still. They would pull a tuft of cotton apart slowly to test the length of the fiber. They would roll a thread between thumb and finger, hold it to the light, sometimes bring it to their nose. They pressed a flat palm on a bale the way you’d check an animal’s heartbeat. No instruments, no digital scales, no lab reports. After thirty or forty years of touching the same material, their fingertips were better sensors than any machine I’ve met since.

I stood next to my father and watched a scene I now think about constantly.

A heavy merchant with a grey mustache and his tarboush pushed back on his head was talking to a buyer from a workshop a few streets away. They talked about the cotton, the season, someone’s cousin just back from abroad. Ten minutes went by before anyone mentioned a price. Then the merchant named a number, the buyer clicked his tongue and named a lower one, the merchant looked at the sky as if the insult had wounded him, and the buyer laughed. They settled somewhere in the middle. The buyer put out his hand, the merchant took it, done.

A truckload of cotton, worth more than many families earn in a year, had just been sold. No paper. No signature, no stamp, no notary. Nobody had said when payment was due, or if they had, it was something loose like “after Eid” or “when you’ve sold the first batch.” The buyer’s men were already loading bales onto a cart while the two of them drank tea and talked about something else.

I asked my father quietly, the way children ask what adults have stopped asking: “What if he doesn’t pay?”

He smiled without looking at me. “Then he won’t buy again. From anyone.”

It sounded simple then. It took me years, and a PhD, to see how complete the answer was.

That was the whole system. The contract was the man’s name, and the court was the town. If a buyer didn’t pay, the story would reach the coffee shops, the workshops and the Friday tables before he got home. Within a week no merchant would sell him thread on credit. Within a month, people who had never met him knew his name and the story attached to it. In a town where everyone is connected to everyone, a broken promise is never private.

So people rarely broke them. They weren’t saints. The cost was just so high and so certain that honesty was the cheaper option.

I watched men build fortunes this way. Quiet men in plain clothes who ended up with workshops of dozens of machines, and who had started by buying one small lot of cotton on credit from a merchant who trusted their word. They paid back early, every time, until one day that merchant offered them ten lots instead of one. No bank had assessed them and no analyst had studied their risk. Their reputation grew slowly, and eventually it could carry real weight.

Years later, in university rooms, I learned the vocabulary for what I had seen as a child: informal institutions, relational contracting, social capital, trust-based governance. I read papers analyzing exactly what those men did by instinct. I remember one lecture where a professor presented these ideas as exotic discoveries, and I smiled to myself, because I had watched them happen with cotton dust in my hair.

The souq taught me something else too, which no lecture covered. I only understood it when I started working for a business owner back in Tunisia.

I won’t name him or say what he sold. The pattern is what matters. He had found one thing that worked: one product, one way of buying, one way of selling, one circle of people he trusted. It succeeded, and from then on it was untouchable. Any idea that didn’t look like the original formula was treated with suspicion. Anyone who arrived with a different method was welcomed politely at the door and kept at a distance. I wouldn’t call it arrogance. It was fear dressed up as experience. He had seen what works and saw no reason to risk it.

I recognized it at once, because I’d seen it in the souq. The trust that made the system strong also made it closed. His fortune was built inside a bubble, the bubble protected it, and the bubble decided who never got in: outsiders, new models, young people with different questions. They stayed outside, politely, forever.

Sitting in his office, I realized something about myself. I admired him, and I respected the instinct behind what he’d built. But when I pictured running a business of my own, I felt nothing. No pull, no hunger to be the name on the door. What drew me was the empty chair beside him. I wanted to be the person who could see what he couldn’t from inside the bubble, and translate his instincts into something he could examine and pass on. I wanted to build around the fortune, not necessarily own it.

That’s the distinction I want to leave you with, because we rarely say it. Our culture insists that anyone with talent and ambition must end up an owner. Nobody tells you that being born to run a business and being born to work with one are different callings, and neither is smaller. The souq in Ksar Hellal needed both: the merchant who held the word of the whole market in his hand, and the people around him who made that word travel and survive.

It took me years to accept which of the two I was. It’s why I study how businesses are designed, why I sit with owners and ask them questions, and why I’m writing this. But that’s another entry.

posts.author: Dr. Mohamed Abdellaziz Hmad
posts.body:
“Moving for opportunities” sounds like a cliché, so let me be specific. It was a real conversation, and it went on for many evenings at the family table. What do we have here? What could we have there? Where does the children’s education lead? Where is there room to grow? Nobody said “strategy.” Looking back, that’s what it was: my parents weighing risk against opportunity with incomplete information, like any business owner.

I was the youngest. That meant I understood the least in the room and noticed the most. My older siblings argued and worried out loud. I sat in the corner with my homework open, listening. Nobody tells a child what is really being decided, but you can feel it when the adults lower their voices.

Leaving a town where everyone knows your name is a big thing. In Ksar Hellal my family had a place. Years of relationships, a reputation that opened doors without anyone asking. Moving meant giving up that credit and arriving as strangers. At university I would learn to call it a reinvestment: you spend the stability you’ve built to buy a chance at growth.

It was a gamble, and for a while nobody knew if it would pay off.

A new city, a new kind of silence

Sousse was bigger and brighter, open to the sea. Tourists, hotels, cafés full of young people. In Ksar Hellal the horizon was the factory wall. In Sousse you could see the water. I think that mattered more than I knew then.

At my new school I was a stranger. Back home I was someone’s son. Here I was a new face in a corridor, and belonging had to be earned again from zero. It was my first lesson in being unknown, years before I left the country.

Then, slowly, the move started to work. There was no single moment I could point to. A door opened here, a contact appeared there, and things steadied. From outside it looked like nothing. From inside it felt like finally breathing out. I remember one evening when the talk at the table changed. The worry was gone. We were asking what we wanted next instead of what we feared.

The family as a business

I only found words for this once I started studying business design.

A family is a business.

I don’t mean that coldly, and I’m not saying love is a transaction. A family just has the same structural problems as any enterprise. Limited resources, and decisions about how to spend them. Long-term goals like education and a home, short-term pressures like bills and emergencies. Roles that have to be clear, or there’s friction. Investments with uncertain returns. And if nobody maintains it, it drifts.

My parents handled all of this without a manual. My father kept a small notebook, worn at the corners, with what came in and what went out. Nobody asked him to. He believed that what you don’t measure, you can’t steer. My mother held the other half: the rhythm of the house, who needed what and when, a thousand small adjustments made before anyone saw a problem. They never called it a system, but it had a budget, a plan, divided roles and a direction.

I once saw them at the table late in the evening with the notebook open between them, talking quietly. Not arguing. Reviewing. What worked this month, what didn’t, what to change next. Swap the kitchen table for a boardroom and nobody would have noticed. It was a business meeting, and the business was us.

What struck me later was how few families see this as management. We think business happens in offices and workshops, and that family runs on instinct and emotion. But the families that do well maintain themselves on purpose. They talk about money honestly, plan for the next stage before it arrives, and adapt instead of defending the old arrangement out of habit.

The ones that struggle often struggle for the same reasons businesses do. Unspoken expectations. Decisions nobody owns. Refusing to change after the old formula stopped working. I had already seen that in the souq, and in the business owner’s bubble.

The question nobody asked

I spent about ten years in the school system, 2011 to 2021. Hundreds of classes, hundreds of students. Without ever deciding to, I became an observer.

What I noticed was that almost nobody had a picture of their future. Not a bad one, not an overambitious one. None. I’d ask a classmate in the corridor what they planned to do after graduating and get a shrug, or “we’ll see,” or the name of a degree as if that explained itself. They studied because it was next. They passed exams because exams existed. Nobody had a sentence in their head that started with “I want to build…” or “I want to become…”

One afternoon we were sitting outside after class, and I asked a friend, a smart guy, what he would actually do with his diploma. He looked at me as if I’d asked something unreasonable.

“Find a job.”

“Which one?”

He laughed. “Whichever one exists.”

That stayed with me for years. It wasn’t laziness. A whole generation had been trained to finish steps without anyone asking where the steps led.

Maybe I noticed because of home. In my family the future got discussed, calculated, planned. It had a notebook. At school it had nothing, and the contrast was too sharp to ignore.

Why the horizon was missing

I’ve thought about this a lot, and I don’t blame the students. The system taught us to answer questions but never to choose which questions matter. We memorized, repeated, passed. Nobody explained how the economy worked outside the classroom: how a business starts, what an employer needs, how value gets created, which skills are worth building. We learned subjects. Nobody connected them to life.

The world was also unsettled. The years after 2011 were full of change, and when the ground shifts, planning feels like a luxury. Many families wanted stability more than ambition. The message, usually unspoken: get the diploma, find something secure, take no risks. I understand it. I also understand the cost, a generation that can follow instructions but has never practiced imagining.

And there was the souq again. Fortunes there were made by people who stayed close to what worked. In the classroom I saw the same thing. Students stuck to the one path they knew because it had worked for someone they knew. The bubble around those business owners existed in school too, only softer and harder to see.

What watching taught me

I never planned to research this. But after years in those rooms I had been collecting data without noticing.

Talent wasn’t the shortage. The students I knew were curious, funny, capable. What they lacked was orientation, someone saying: here’s how the world works, here’s where you could fit, here are options you haven’t seen. You can’t choose a future you’ve never been shown.

I learned something about myself too. I was the odd one who kept asking why and what for, about the world behind the curriculum, and I felt a bit alone doing it. That was uncomfortable. It was also a signal. The questions I couldn’t drop were pointing somewhere.

Later, working with business owners as a business designer, I saw the same pattern again. Owners with years of experience who had never sat down and drawn what the business was for or where it was going. Companies running on habit the way those students ran on routine. The classroom and the workshop had more in common than anyone admits.

That’s when it clicked. What I noticed as a teenager and what I solve for businesses now are one problem: people and organizations moving without a design, following steps with no picture of the destination.

A note for anyone still in that classroom

If you’re a student and you don’t know what you want to do, here is what nobody told me: not knowing is normal. It isn’t a flaw. It’s what you get when you’re trained for answers but not for direction.

Don’t leave it there, though. Start asking the questions nobody asks you. What do people actually pay for? What problems around me are unsolved? What would I do if the diploma were the starting point and not the goal? You won’t answer them all at once. I didn’t. I answered them slowly, by watching, asking, and working near people who build things.

The first organization you’ll ever manage is your own life, and later maybe your family. Treat it as worth designing early and it runs better.

The future isn’t waiting at the end of a degree. You design it. Start sketching now, even badly, and more of it will be yours.
posts.title: The Classroom with no Horizon
posts.subtitle: In 2011 Tunisia changed, and for my family that meant a decision. We left Ksar Hellal for Sousse. Nothing was wrong. We just wanted something better.
